Confirmed, not a [GAP]: the EU's core pet-import mechanics (microchip, rabies vaccination timing, titer-test-if-unlisted, Animal Health Certificate, no quarantine if compliant) apply identically to dogs, cats, and ferrets — all three are treated uniformly as the species covered by Annex I, Part A of the governing regulation. The one real, sourced divergence found: the EU's Echinococcus multilocularis (tapeworm) treatment requirement (praziquantel or equivalent, 24-120 hours before entry) applies to dogs ONLY — cats and ferrets are explicitly exempt — but this treatment is itself only required by a named short list of destination states (Finland, Ireland, Malta, UK via Northern Ireland, Norway), and Greece is not one of them, so the divergence doesn't actually change anything for a cat or dog entering Crete specifically

fact_label: Pet import (dog) — dangerous-breed restriction status, unresolved

fact_label: Pet import (dog) — rabies titer / quarantine requirement
value_raw: No titer test and no quarantine for a dog departing from a listed third country (US, UK, Canada, and Australia all confirmed listed) with a compliant microchip + rabies vaccination (12+ weeks old, 21-day wait) + Animal Health Certificate (valid 10 days). Departing from an unlisted country instead requires a titer test — blood drawn 30+ days after primary vaccination, tested at a designated lab, certificate not issuable until 90+ days after the sample was drawn. No quarantine either way once documentation is complete and correctly sequenced; incomplete/incorrect paperwork can get a pet held or refused at the Border Inspection Post instead

date: 2004-04-29 (Directive 2004/38/EC adopted; transposition deadline 2006-04-30; consolidated text current through amending Directive 2011/24/EU, in force 2011-06-16)
document_conditional_note: Residence beyond three months requires meeting one of several conditions (Directive 2004/38/EC Art. 7): being a worker or self-employed, having sufficient resources plus comprehensive health insurance, being an enrolled student with resources and insurance, or being a qualifying family member of someone who meets one of those. This is an additional, better-secured right some readers can go on to claim -- it is never a condition on the entry/short-stay tier shown above, which is already unconditionally true for up to three months under Art. 6 ("without any conditions or any formalities other than the requirement to hold a valid identity card or passport"). A host state may ask for registration after arrival (Art. 8), but the Directive states plainly that holding a registration certificate "may under no circumstances be made a precondition for the exercise of a right" -- a formality, not a gate.
